transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, um… thanks. I guess what brings me in is that I’ve been having a hard time shaking this feeling—well, more than a feeling, honestly—that certain people around here, mostly in the arts and finance circles in Cincinnati, are keeping track of me.

Like, not openly. It’s subtle. I work as a financial advisor, so I meet with clients, go to events, panels, receptions, that kind of thing, and it’s started to seem like some people know who I’ve been meeting with or are watching the pattern of it. Then I’ll get an invitation to something, or there’ll be a panel topic that feels oddly specific, or someone will sit near me at an event in a way that feels arranged. Little things like that. And I know, I know how it sounds—I do try to tell myself maybe it’s coincidence, maybe I’m reading into it—but I can’t really let it go once I notice it. It kind of stays with me and I keep turning it over in my head.
How long have you been noticing and feeling concerned about these patterns of being watched or tracked—weeks, months, or longer?

I’d say it’s been about two months, maybe a little over if I’m being really exact. It wasn’t like one day I woke up and thought, “Okay, this is happening.” It sort of built up.

At first it was just noticing odd overlaps—like I’d meet with a client or have a conversation, and then something at an event or in an email invitation would feel like it was pointing back to that. But around two months ago is when it started feeling consistent enough that I couldn’t just brush it off. That’s when I started really paying attention to the idea that people might be tracking who I’m meeting with and kind of sending signals through those situations.
Have you experienced anything like hearing voices, sounds, or seeing things that others don't seem to notice, along with these feelings of being watched?

I don’t think so… not in the sense of, like, hearing a voice talking to me or seeing a person there that other people can’t see. I haven’t had anything like that, at least not that I’d call that.

There are times at events where I’ll notice a sound or a bit of conversation from across the room and I’ll wonder if it’s connected to me, but that’s more me interpreting what’s happening around me, I guess. It’s not like I’m hearing something that no one else could hear. And visually, no, I don’t think I’ve seen things that weren’t there. It’s more the patterns and the timing of things that get to me.
Before these last two months, would you say you've generally been a trusting person, or have you tended to be wary and suspicious of others' motives for most of your adult life?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I wouldn’t have described myself as suspicious, exactly. I mean, in finance you kind of have to be careful with people’s motives, right? You’re trained to pay attention to incentives, conflicts of interest, what someone stands to gain, whether something is being presented a certain way. So I’ve probably always been… analytical, maybe guarded in a professional sense.

But in my personal life, I don’t think I went around assuming people were against me or anything like that. I had normal doubts about people sometimes, like anyone does, but I don’t remember feeling this kind of constant need to connect the dots or figure out whether something was aimed at me. That feels more recent. At least, that’s how it seems to me now.

Aside from these suspicions, has your ability to do your job, manage daily responsibilities, and interact with family or friends stayed pretty much the same as before, or have you noticed a decline in how you're functioning overall?

It’s… mostly the same on the surface, in the sense that I’m still working and I’m still handling basic day-to-day things. I’m not, you know, unable to get out of bed or completely dropping everything. But if I’m being honest, there has been some decline professionally.

My practice has gotten smaller than it was, and part of that is because I’ve been missing follow-ups or putting them off longer than I normally would. I used to be pretty consistent about staying in touch with clients, checking in, keeping the relationship warm, that kind of thing. Lately it takes more effort, and sometimes I avoid reaching out if I’m not sure how the interaction is going to feel or what might come from it.

I’ve also avoided some public panels and events I probably would have done before. Those used to be useful for networking and visibility, and I know skipping them doesn’t help my business. But I find myself backing out or not volunteering for things like that as much.

So, I wouldn’t say everything has fallen apart, but I’m not functioning at quite the same level I was. Especially with keeping up client contact and follow-through. That’s where I notice it most.

Have you noticed any changes in your emotional expression or motivation—like feeling emotionally flat, losing interest in things you used to enjoy, or having less energy or drive—since this all started?

Yeah… I think so, though it’s a little hard for me to separate what’s emotional from what’s just being tired or preoccupied.

I’m still doing things, but it’s more in pieces. Like with work, I’ll handle the urgent things, I’ll respond when I really have to, but I don’t have the same push I used to have. Client follow-ups will just sit there longer than they should, and I’ll know I should make the call or send the email, but it feels like this extra weight to start it. Before, I was more proactive. I had more of a spark, I guess.

Outside of work, yeah, I’ve been skipping things I normally liked. I used to go to jazz nights sometimes, or play pickup basketball, and now I’ll just not go. And the weird part is I don’t always feel that disappointed about missing it. It’s not like, “Oh no, I wish I’d gone.” It’s more like… nothing. Or just, “That would take effort.”

And with friends, when they ask what’s going on, I give these short answers. Not because I’m trying to be rude, but talking feels like more effort than it should. Explaining myself feels exhausting, so I’ll say, “I’m fine,” or “Just busy,” and leave it there. I don’t know if I’d call it emotionally flat exactly, but I do feel less engaged than I usually am.

Before these suspicions started about two months ago, did you notice any earlier changes—like being less motivated, more withdrawn, or just not feeling like yourself—going back further, maybe four to six months or more?

Yeah… I think maybe it did start before the suspiciousness got really noticeable. Not in a dramatic way, though. It wasn’t like one day I suddenly stopped functioning or anything. It was more like I was still doing what I needed to do, but only in pieces, if that makes sense.

Like with work, I could still handle the things that were urgent or right in front of me, but I didn’t have the same spark I used to have. I’d let client follow-ups sit longer than I normally would, and then I’d feel this sort of resistance to starting them. Not even because the task was complicated — it’s just a phone call, an email, a check-in — but it felt heavier than it should have.

And outside of work, I started skipping things I used to actually enjoy, like jazz nights or pickup basketball. Before, those were easy yeses for me, or at least things I’d look forward to. But I’d find myself just not going, and the strange part is I didn’t feel that much about missing them. It wasn’t like I was upset or guilty. It was more just… blank, or like, “Okay, I didn’t go.”

With friends too, I think I got more withdrawn. If someone asked what was going on, I’d give short answers — “I’m fine,” “just busy,” whatever. Not because I didn’t care about them, but talking felt like it took more effort than it should. So yeah, looking back, there probably were some changes before the last two months. I just didn’t really label them as anything at the time.

Along with this drop in motivation and interest, have you also been feeling persistently sad, hopeless, or down on yourself—like an actual low mood—or is it more just a lack of drive without that emotional sadness?

I don’t know that I’d call it a low mood, exactly. I mean, I have moments where I feel frustrated with myself, because I know I’m not doing things the way I normally would, and then I’ll think, “Why is this so hard?” But it doesn’t feel like I’m walking around sad all day or crying or feeling hopeless in that kind of way.

It’s more like the engine isn’t turning over. Like I can see the thing I’m supposed to do, and part of me understands why it matters, but there’s not much momentum behind it. And with things I used to enjoy, it’s not always that they feel miserable or pointless — it’s more that the interest just isn’t there the same way, or it feels like too much effort to get myself started.

So… no, not persistently sad, I don’t think. More flat, maybe, or stalled. And then I get down on myself in little bursts because I’m aware of it, but I wouldn’t say the main feeling is sadness.

Thinking back, would you say these changes in your motivation, energy, and interest in activities have been going on fairly continuously for six months or more, or did they come and go during that time?

Honestly, looking back, I think it’s been more continuous than I wanted to admit. Not exactly the same intensity the whole time, but it’s been building for a long time — probably since that arts nonprofit recognition thing a little over two years ago.

At the time I didn’t think of it as “motivation problems” or anything like that. I just thought maybe I was tired, or maybe that whole period took more out of me than I realized. But after that, little by little, I started feeling less like myself. I was still functioning, still working, still showing up enough that from the outside it probably didn’t look that dramatic. But the extra drive, the initiative, the wanting to do things — that started fading.

It would come in waves a little, where some weeks I could push through better than others, but I don’t think it fully went away. It’s more like there’s been this baseline of lower energy and less interest that’s been there, and then recently it’s become more obvious because I’m noticing how much I’m avoiding or putting off. So yeah… not just the last few months. I’d say it’s been building pretty steadily for over two years.

Have you or people close to you noticed any changes in how you organize your thoughts or express yourself—like your speech becoming hard to follow, jumping between unrelated topics, or your behavior seeming unusual or disorganized to others?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’ve noticed anything like my speech being… totally hard to follow or me bouncing from one subject to something completely unrelated. At least nobody has sat me down and said, “You’re not making sense,” or anything that direct.

Sometimes I probably explain things in a more roundabout way than I need to, especially if I’m trying to justify why I did or didn’t do something. Like I’ll give a lot of background, and then halfway through I realize maybe the other person just asked a simple question. But I’ve kind of always been someone who explains too much, especially at work, because I’m used to walking clients through details. So I don’t know if that’s a change or just me.

As far as behavior seeming disorganized… I don’t think so? I might be more scattered with following through on things, like starting something and then delaying it, but that feels more like difficulty getting myself moving than not knowing what I’m doing. My thoughts can feel cluttered sometimes, but I can usually get them across if I slow down. So no, I wouldn’t say people have told me I’m talking strangely or acting really disorganized.

Besides the feeling of being watched or tracked, have you had any other unusual beliefs or experiences—like feeling your thoughts are being read, controlled, or broadcast, or that you have some special importance or ability that others don't recognize?

Not really in the sense of, like, my thoughts being read or controlled. I don’t think someone is putting thoughts in my head or broadcasting them or anything like that. And I don’t think I have some special power.

It’s more specific than that, and it’s part of why I came in, honestly. For a while now I’ve had this conviction that certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are sort of… quietly tracking me. Not tracking like with a device necessarily, but watching which clients I meet with, who I’m connected to, where I show up. And then I’ll notice things that feel like signals — like an invitation arriving right after I meet with someone, or a panel topic that seems too closely connected to something I just discussed, or even who ends up sitting near me at an event.

And I know how that sounds. I can say to myself, “Okay, maybe that’s just coincidence, maybe you’re reading into it.” But it doesn’t really settle. I can’t quite let it go, because the timing and the pattern feel too specific sometimes. It’s like there’s this layer of communication happening around me that nobody is saying directly, but I’m supposed to notice it.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about reduced emotional expression, motivation, interest, energy, and drive, which directly matches Negative_Symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so, though it’s a little hard for me to separate what’s emotional from what’s just being tired or preoccupied.

I’m still doing things, but it’s more in pieces. Like with work, I’ll handle the urgent things, I’ll respond when I really have to, but I don’t have the same push I used to have. Client follow-ups will just sit there longer than they should, and I’ll know I should make the call or send the email, but it feels like this extra weight to start it. Before, I was more proactive. I had more of a spark, I guess.

Outside of work, yeah, I’ve been skipping things I normally liked. I used to go to jazz nights sometimes, or play pickup basketball, and now I’ll just not go. And the weird part is I don’t always feel that disappointed about missing it. It’s not like, “Oh no, I wish I’d gone.” It’s more like… nothing. Or just, “That would take effort.”

And with friends, when they ask what’s going on, I give these short answers. Not because I’m trying to be rude, but talking feels like more effort than it should. Explaining myself feels exhausting, so I’ll say, “I’m fine,” or “Just busy,” and leave it there. I don’t know if I’d call it emotionally flat exactly, but I do feel less engaged than I usually am.

inference.note: Emerging negative symptoms (anhedonia, avolition, blunted affect) alongside encapsulated persecutory beliefs support continued consideration of both an isolated delusional disorder (F22) and early schizophrenia (F20.0) with prodromal negative symptoms; no hallucinations reported, keeping other psychotic spectrum disorders less likely.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was any earlier prodromal period of subtle behavioral, motivational, or social changes before the 2-month mark, to assess if total duration of disturbance approaches or exceeds 6 months (key for schizophrenia vs. delusional disorder)
doctor.question: Before these suspicions started about two months ago, did you notice any earlier changes—like being less motivated, more withdrawn, or just not feeling like yourself—going back further, maybe four to six months or more?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I still get my work done in pieces, but I don’t have the same spark—I’ll leave client follow-ups sitting, skip jazz nights or pickup basketball without much feeling about it, and when friends ask what’s going on I give short answers because talking feels like more effort than it should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about earlier changes in motivation, withdrawal, and not feeling like himself, which directly matches negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think maybe it did start before the suspiciousness got really noticeable. Not in a dramatic way, though. It wasn’t like one day I suddenly stopped functioning or anything. It was more like I was still doing what I needed to do, but only in pieces, if that makes sense.

Like with work, I could still handle the things that were urgent or right in front of me, but I didn’t have the same spark I used to have. I’d let client follow-ups sit longer than I normally would, and then I’d feel this sort of resistance to starting them. Not even because the task was complicated — it’s just a phone call, an email, a check-in — but it felt heavier than it should have.

And outside of work, I started skipping things I used to actually enjoy, like jazz nights or pickup basketball. Before, those were easy yeses for me, or at least things I’d look forward to. But I’d find myself just not going, and the strange part is I didn’t feel that much about missing them. It wasn’t like I was upset or guilty. It was more just… blank, or like, “Okay, I didn’t go.”

With friends too, I think I got more withdrawn. If someone asked what was going on, I’d give short answers — “I’m fine,” “just busy,” whatever. Not because I didn’t care about them, but talking felt like it took more effort than it should. So yeah, looking back, there probably were some changes before the last two months. I just didn’t really label them as anything at the time.

inference.note: The description of negative symptoms (anhedonia, avolition, blunted affect, social withdrawal) predating and co-occurring with the persecutory delusions, along with functional decline, argues against isolated delusional disorder (F22) and favors a schizophrenia-spectrum process (F20.0). Because these negative/mood-like symptoms are prominent and temporally intertwined with the psychotic features, schizoaffective disorder, depressive type (F25.1) is now also considered.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced core depressive mood symptoms (sadness, hopelessness, worthlessness, guilt) rather than just reduced motivation/energy, to distinguish a true mood episode (favoring schizoaffective disorder) from negative symptoms of schizophrenia
doctor.question: Along with this drop in motivation and interest, have you also been feeling persistently sad, hopeless, or down on yourself—like an actual low mood—or is it more just a lack of drive without that emotional sadness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistently sad, hopeless, or low mood to distinguish depression from low motivation; the provided symptom profile includes negative symptoms but does not include depressive mood symptoms.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d call it a low mood, exactly. I mean, I have moments where I feel frustrated with myself, because I know I’m not doing things the way I normally would, and then I’ll think, “Why is this so hard?” But it doesn’t feel like I’m walking around sad all day or crying or feeling hopeless in that kind of way.

It’s more like the engine isn’t turning over. Like I can see the thing I’m supposed to do, and part of me understands why it matters, but there’s not much momentum behind it. And with things I used to enjoy, it’s not always that they feel miserable or pointless — it’s more that the interest just isn’t there the same way, or it feels like too much effort to get myself started.

So… no, not persistently sad, I don’t think. More flat, maybe, or stalled. And then I get down on myself in little bursts because I’m aware of it, but I wouldn’t say the main feeling is sadness.

inference.note: Patient denies persistent low mood or hopelessness, arguing against a mood component needed for schizoaffective disorder (F25.1), so it is replaced with delusional disorder (F22) as an alternative given the encapsulated persecutory beliefs without hallucinations, though prominent negative symptoms and functional decline still favor schizophrenia (F20.0).

doctor.intent: Determine whether the negative symptoms (avolition, blunted affect, anhedonia) and functional decline have persisted continuously for at least 6 months, which is required to distinguish schizophrenia (F20.0) from delusional disorder (F22) where functioning is typically preserved outside the delusion's impact
doctor.question: Thinking back, would you say these changes in your motivation, energy, and interest in activities have been going on fairly continuously for six months or more, or did they come and go during that time?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: These changes have been building since that arts nonprofit recognition a little over two years ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the changes in motivation, energy, and interest have been present and whether they have persisted for six months or more.

patient.answer:
Honestly, looking back, I think it’s been more continuous than I wanted to admit. Not exactly the same intensity the whole time, but it’s been building for a long time — probably since that arts nonprofit recognition thing a little over two years ago.

At the time I didn’t think of it as “motivation problems” or anything like that. I just thought maybe I was tired, or maybe that whole period took more out of me than I realized. But after that, little by little, I started feeling less like myself. I was still functioning, still working, still showing up enough that from the outside it probably didn’t look that dramatic. But the extra drive, the initiative, the wanting to do things — that started fading.

It would come in waves a little, where some weeks I could push through better than others, but I don’t think it fully went away. It’s more like there’s been this baseline of lower energy and less interest that’s been there, and then recently it’s become more obvious because I’m noticing how much I’m avoiding or putting off. So yeah… not just the last few months. I’d say it’s been building pretty steadily for over two years.

inference.note: The persistent >2-year history of avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal, and functional decline alongside 2 months of persecutory delusions supports schizophrenia (F20.0), since this pattern of prodromal negative symptoms plus active delusional phase exceeds the isolated, functionally-preserved presentation typical of delusional disorder (F22), which remains possible but less likely given the degree of functional and negative symptom involvement.

doctor.intent: Assess for disorganized thinking or behavior (another core symptom domain of schizophrenia) to help distinguish schizophrenia from delusional disorder, which requires isolated delusions without other psychotic features
doctor.question: Have you or people close to you noticed any changes in how you organize your thoughts or express yourself—like your speech becoming hard to follow, jumping between unrelated topics, or your behavior seeming unusual or disorganized to others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorganized thinking, speech, or behavior, but the provided symptom profile does not include a disorganized symptoms item.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I mean, I don’t think I’ve noticed anything like my speech being… totally hard to follow or me bouncing from one subject to something completely unrelated. At least nobody has sat me down and said, “You’re not making sense,” or anything that direct.

Sometimes I probably explain things in a more roundabout way than I need to, especially if I’m trying to justify why I did or didn’t do something. Like I’ll give a lot of background, and then halfway through I realize maybe the other person just asked a simple question. But I’ve kind of always been someone who explains too much, especially at work, because I’m used to walking clients through details. So I don’t know if that’s a change or just me.

As far as behavior seeming disorganized… I don’t think so? I might be more scattered with following through on things, like starting something and then delaying it, but that feels more like difficulty getting myself moving than not knowing what I’m doing. My thoughts can feel cluttered sometimes, but I can usually get them across if I slow down. So no, I wouldn’t say people have told me I’m talking strangely or acting really disorganized.

inference.note: No evidence of disorganized speech/behavior or hallucinations, supporting either delusional disorder or schizophrenia with prominent negative symptoms; chronic negative symptoms (>2 years) alongside 2-month delusional preoccupation keep both diagnoses viable.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's psychotic symptoms are limited to a single, circumscribed non-bizarre belief (favoring delusional disorder) or involve broader/bizarre psychotic content such as thought interference, grandiosity, or other unusual beliefs (favoring schizophrenia)
doctor.question: Besides the feeling of being watched or tracked, have you had any other unusual beliefs or experiences—like feeling your thoughts are being read, controlled, or broadcast, or that you have some special importance or ability that others don't recognize?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because for a while now I’ve been convinced that certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with and sending me little signals through invitations, panel topics, even who sits near me at events, and even when I tell myself it could just be coincidence, I can’t really let it go.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about other unusual fixed beliefs or psychotic-like beliefs, such as thought broadcasting, control, or special significance, which falls under delusions.

patient.answer:
Not really in the sense of, like, my thoughts being read or controlled. I don’t think someone is putting thoughts in my head or broadcasting them or anything like that. And I don’t think I have some special power.

It’s more specific than that, and it’s part of why I came in, honestly. For a while now I’ve had this conviction that certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are sort of… quietly tracking me. Not tracking like with a device necessarily, but watching which clients I meet with, who I’m connected to, where I show up. And then I’ll notice things that feel like signals — like an invitation arriving right after I meet with someone, or a panel topic that seems too closely connected to something I just discussed, or even who ends up sitting near me at an event.

And I know how that sounds. I can say to myself, “Okay, maybe that’s just coincidence, maybe you’re reading into it.” But it doesn’t really settle. I can’t quite let it go, because the timing and the pattern feel too specific sometimes. It’s like there’s this layer of communication happening around me that nobody is saying directly, but I’m supposed to notice it.

inference.note: The patient reports over two years of gradually worsening avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal, and functional decline preceding and continuing alongside two months of persistent, systematized persecutory delusions. This pattern—prominent negative symptoms plus active-phase delusions lasting more than a month, with clear functional decline—fits the broader symptom and duration criteria for schizophrenia rather than an isolated delusional disorder, which requires delusions without other schizophrenia-spectrum features like negative symptoms or significant functional deterioration. F22 is therefore no longer supported.

Importantly, these delusions emerged against a backdrop of over two years of prodromal negative symptoms—avolition, anhedonia, blunted affect, and social/occupational withdrawal—with clear functional decline in his professional and personal life. The combination of active-phase delusions (positive symptom criterion A) plus a prolonged prodromal/residual phase with negative symptoms and functional deterioration exceeding 6 months supports a diagnosis of Schizophrenia, Paranoid Type (F20.0) rather than Delusional Disorder (F22, which requires absence of negative symptoms/functional decline) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (mood symptoms are secondary and lack pervasive sadness/hopelessness, ruling out F25.1).
